# Presenting characteristics and clinical outcomes of idiopathic versus neurofibromatosis type 2–associated spinal meningiomas: a retrospective institutional experience

**Authors:** Noah L. A. Nawabi; Joshua I. Chalif; Sophia Renauld; Neel H. Mehta; Rohan Jha; Jakob V. E. Gerstl; Eric Chalif; Saksham Gupta; John H. Chi

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Neurosurgery, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | 2College of Medicine, Medical University of South Carolina, Charleston, South Carolina | 3Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts

## Abstract

Spinal meningioma (SM) is a pathology with an estimated incidence of nearly 1000 diagnoses per year in the United States and presents in 20% of patients with neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2). This multi-institutional retrospective cohort study aimed to assess clinical outcomes for patients with SM who underwent surgery between 1998 and 2020 with stratification by NF2 mutation status.

Medical records were reviewed retrospectively to collect data on patient demographics, clinical presentation, tumor characteristics, treatment, and outcomes. Analyses were done to determine radiographic predictors of gross-total resection (GTR) and tumor recurrence, to assess radiographic characteristics of NF2-associated tumors, and to determine progression-free survival between groups.

A total of 166 patients who received surgery for SM during the study period were included, of whom 133 were women (80%). Fifteen (9%) patients had a concurrent NF2 diagnosis. The mean age at surgery was 58 (SD 18) years. The mean presenting Karnofsky Performance Status score was 76 (SD 11), and the most common presenting symptoms were sensation changes (60%) and weakness (59%). Most tumors were in the thoracic spine (72%). GTR was achieved in 154 cases (93%). Eight patients with subtotal resection were treated with radiation therapy, and none received chemotherapy. Eighteen patients (11%) experienced radiographic recurrence of disease following surgery, with a mean time to recurrence of 4.2 years. NF2 patients were diagnosed at a significantly earlier mean age (33.3 [SD 15.4] years) compared with other patients. NF2 patients experienced progression at a significantly higher rate than other patients (40%), and in less time (mean 2.8 [SD 3.7] years). Radiographic characteristics, including tumor volume, T2 cord edema, dural tail sign, and calcification, were similar between NF2 and non-NF2 patients, between patients who underwent gross-total versus subtotal resection, and between patients who experienced tumor recurrence and those who did not.

In this study of 166 surgically treated patients with SM, patients with NF2 presented earlier, experienced earlier progression, and experienced progression more frequently compared with those without NF2. Radiographic characteristics of tumors were relatively consistent between groups. While idiopathic SMs remain a relatively benign and highly manageable disease, considering tumor molecular characteristics and broader clinical history is paramount in providing efficacious and individualized patient care.

Spinal meningiomas (SMs) are among the most common primary spinal tumors in adults, accounting for 25%–40% of all intradural spinal neoplasms despite accounting for only 2%–12% of all meningioma diagnoses.1,2 Clinically, SMs often present with generalized weakness, sensory impairment, progressive myelopathy, and acute or chronic pain.3 Classically, SM treatment involves resection of the tumor, with gross-total resection (GTR) rates approaching 90% and often yielding symptomatic resolution with limited complications.2 SMs are often relatively benign pathologically, and GTR or near-GTR often yields complete freedom of disease, leaving patients without the need for regular long-term follow-up.4

Although SMs often present as idiopathic tumors in adults, they are also a relatively common finding in patients with a diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2). NF2 is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by de novo mutations of the tumor suppressor gene NF2, which predisposes patients to the development of recurrent and complex CNS tumors, including bilateral vestibular schwannomas, multiple intracranial meningiomas, and SMs in up to 20% of all NF2 patients.5 Because of the often-severe tumor burden associated with NF2, SMs associated with a concurrent diagnosis of NF2 may warrant different clinical management compared with patients presenting with idiopathic SMs.

However, differences in radiographic features and presenting characteristics of NF2-associated versus idiopathic SMs in otherwise healthy patients are currently unclear, as are their potential impacts on achieving maximal resection and other favorable clinical outcomes. Furthermore, current treatment guidelines centered around how management should be longitudinally altered for SM patients with idiopathic tumors versus those patients with SM and progressive diseases such as NF2 are ambiguous.6 In the present study, we report on a large cohort of SM patients stratified into groups based on a concurrent diagnosis of NF2. Differences in clinical presentation, radiographic and molecular tumor characteristics, surgical outcomes, and disease trajectory between these two groups were explored. We aimed to identify factors that have the potential to impact surgical management and long-term clinical outcomes of patients with SMs.

## Methods

### Patient Selection

Patients with a diagnosis of SM between 1998 and 2020 were identified using ICD-10 codes utilizing Mass General Brigham’s Research Patient Database Registry. Patients were excluded if they had incomplete medical records or if they were initially treated surgically at an outside institution.

### Data Collection

Patient medical records were retrospectively reviewed to collect demographical patient data, presentation data, tumor traits including radiographic, pathological, and molecular characteristics, treatment characteristics, and outcome data including functional outcomes, symptomatic progression, recurrence rates, and subsequent treatment. Extent of resection was determined by assessing operative notes and postoperative MRI reports. GTR was defined as no sign of residual disease on initial postoperative MRI. Mention of duraplasty in the operative note was not required for a resection to be labeled a GTR; cauterization of the dura to allow for primary closure was sufficient. Patients were also screened for a history of NF2. For patients with NF2, data on systemic tumor burden and previous treatments were collected.

### Pathology and Cytology

Pathology reports were reviewed to confirm a diagnosis of SM following tumor resection. All reports were reviewed by Massachusetts General Hospital or Brigham and Women’s Hospital pathology departments. Patients with an absent pathology report or unconfirmed diagnosis of SM were excluded. Tumors were graded according to WHO tumor classifications. Cytology and genomics data were collected for all available tumors to assess for chromosomal abnormalities and other genetic disease characteristics.

### Statistical Analysis

All statistical analyses were conducted in R (The R Foundation for Statistical Computing) and GraphPad Prism. The latter was also used to generate figures. Demographic data were summarized as mean and SD, or count and percentage, as appropriate. Unpaired t-tests with Welch’s correction were conducted to compare mean values between the NF2 and idiopathic SM groups. Fisher’s exact tests were conducted to assess the association of an NF2 diagnosis with various radiographic characteristics and to assess the association between the presence of various radiographic characteristics and achieving GTR. Kaplan-Meier survival analyses and curves were constructed to compare overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with NF2 patients versus those with idiopathic SM, and between patients with a grade 1 versus a grade 2 tumor. The mean follow-up time, defined as time from initial surgery to last known date alive based on the electronic medical record, was also calculated and compared between groups.

## Results

### Presenting and Radiographic Characteristics

A total of 224 patients with SM were identified through our institutional query. After exclusion criteria were applied, 166 patients (133 females, 80%) were included. One hundred fifty-one (91%) patients had idiopathic SM, and 15 (9%) patients had an NF2 diagnosis. Fourteen (93%) of the 15 NF2 patients had intracranial meningiomas, 10 (67%) had bilateral vestibular schwannomas, and 1 (7%) had an intracranial ependymoma. Fourteen (93%) of the 15 NF2 patients had a history of at least one intracranial tumor resection. Of note, 9 (6%) of the idiopathic SM patients had a history of intracranial meningioma(s). The mean age at surgery for all patients was 58.3 (SD 18.2) years. Patients with idiopathic SM were diagnosed with their SM at a mean age of 60.8 (SD 17.2) years, compared with a mean of 33.3 (SD 15.4) years in the NF2 group (p < 0.0001) (Fig. 1A). The most common presenting symptoms were loss or alteration in sensation, (n = 100, 60%), weakness (n = 98, 59%), and back pain (n = 59, 36%). The mean presenting Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) score was 76.0 (SD 11). Presenting mean KPS scores were similar between the idiopathic SM and NF2 groups (idiopathic: 76.1 [SD 11.1], NF2: 75.3 [SD 11.1]; p = 0.85) (Fig. 1B). Forty-eight (29%) tumors were located in the cervical spine, 119 (72%) in the thoracic spine, 6 (4%) in the lumbar spine, and 1 (1%) in the sacral spine. Forty-nine (30%) tumors were single-level tumors, and 117 (70%) tumors were multilevel, with most multilevel tumors occurring in the thoracic spine (n = 83, 71%) (Table 1).

Sixteen (10%) tumors were ventrally located with respect to the spinal cord, 20 (12%) were dorsal, 35 (21%) were ventrolateral, 33 (20%) were dorsolateral, 19 (11%) were lateral, and 43 (26%) had unknown laterality due to a lack of the availability of preoperative imaging. The mean tumor volume in the idiopathic SM group was 3.4 (SD 4.7) cm3 compared with 5.2 (SD 6.2) cm3 in the NF2 group (p = 0.43) (Fig. 2A). The mean tumor volume for the whole cohort was 3.5 (SD 4.9) cm3. Fifty-three (35%) of the idiopathic tumors were associated with T2 MRI cord signal change on preoperative imaging, compared with 4 (27%) tumors in the NF2 group (p = 0.58) (Fig. 2B). Thirty-nine (26%) tumors in the idiopathic SM group had a positive dural tail sign on preoperative postcontrast T1-weighted MR images compared with 4 (27%) in the NF2 group (p > 0.99) (Fig. 2C). Fifty-eight (38%) tumors in the idiopathic SM group were calcified based on preoperative CT scans and operative notes, compared with 4 (27%) in the NF2 group (p = 0.42) (Fig. 2D). The remainder of the presenting and radiographic characteristics of the whole cohort, idiopathic SM group, and NF2 group are shown in Table 1.

### Treatment and Outcomes

As expected, the most common laminectomy sites were thoracic (n = 123, 74%) given that most of the tumors were in the thoracic spine. Eleven (7%) were single-level laminectomies and 156 (94%) were multilevel. Nine (5%) patients underwent fusion following their resection. In 1 of these cases, a ventral tumor location in the cervical spine required a corpectomy, thus necessitating fusion. In 2 other cases, fusions were indicated due to the use of multilevel cervical laminectomies. In the remaining 6 fusion cases, particularly high amounts of bony destruction and/or bone removal secondary to the tumor or selected approach necessitated subsequent fusion. Thirty-four (20%) patients had at least one nerve root sacrificed intraoperatively. The mean intraoperative blood loss was 219 (SD 178.3) mL in the total cohort (idiopathic: 204 [SD 147] mL, NF2: 368 [SD 331.7] mL; p = 0.002) (Table 2).

Twelve (7%) patients experienced surgical complications. Persistent CSF leaks in 5 (3%) patients, epidural hematomas in 2 (1%) patients, and a case of cord detethering at the surgical site in 1 (1%) patient required reoperation. One (1%) patient experienced a stroke postoperatively, 1 (1%) patient experienced a subarachnoid hemorrhage at the surgical site, 1 (1%) patient experienced a wound infection, and 1 (1%) patient experienced wound dehiscence. Five patients (3.0%) experienced a new postoperative neurological deficit, 2 of which were new incontinence and 3 of which were new postoperative weakness. Of the 2 cases of new incontinence, 1 had resolved by 1 month postoperatively and the other continued throughout the entirety of the 6-month follow-up period. Of the patients with new postoperative weakness, 2 were noted to have mildly decreased strength in the lower extremities compared with their preoperative levels, and 1 was noted to have significantly decreased strength in the lower extremities, although the latter patient’s weakness was noted to be possibly secondary to a psychiatric concern. One patient with new mild weakness had resolution of symptoms at 6 months, while the other 2 patients continued to experience weakness throughout the entirety of the 6-month follow-up period. Eighty-three (50%) patients reported significant symptomatic improvement in their preoperative symptoms at follow-up, 73 (44%) reported mild improvement, 3 (2%) reported mild worsening, 1 (1%) reported significant worsening, and 6 (4%) reported no change in symptoms (Table 2). Of the 98 patients who presented with weakness, 75 (77%) returned to full strength at follow-up and 10 (10%) had only mild improvements in their strength. We were unable to determine the extent of strength improvement at first follow-up in 13 patients due to missing data in the medical records.

In the idiopathic SM group, 141 (93%) had a GTR compared with 13 (87%) in the NF2 group (p = 0.3) (Fig. 3A). In the idiopathic SM group, 125 (83%) tumors were WHO grade 1, and 15 (10%) were grade 2. In the NF2 group, 10 (67%) tumors were grade 1 and 3 (20%) were grade 2 (p = 0.18) (Fig. 3B). The WHO grade was not reported in the medical records of 11 patients with idiopathic SM and 2 patients with NF2. No patients received chemotherapy for their initial SM. Of the 12 patients with a subtotal resection (STR), 6 (50%) received radiation therapy for residual tumor. Eighteen (11%) patients exhibited radiographic progression of disease, including 12 (8%) in the idiopathic SM group and 6 (40%) in the NF2 group (p = 0.0019) (Fig. 3C). The mean age at progression was 52.4 (SD 24.3) years. The mean times to progression were 4.9 (SD 3.6) years in the idiopathic SM group and 2.8 (SD 3.7) years in the NF2 group (p = 0.28) (Fig. 3D). Of the 18 patients who experienced progression, 11 (61%) underwent a subsequent reoperation (100% GTR), 2 (11%) received post-progression chemotherapy, and 7 (39%) received post-progression radiation therapy (Table 2).

The mean KPS score at last follow-up for the whole cohort was 73.9 (SD 28.7). The mean final KPS for idiopathic SM patients was 75.5 (SD 27.7) compared with 58 (SD 35.1) for NF2 patients (p = 0.67). The mean follow-up time was 8.3 (SD 6.0) years for all SM patients (8.0 [SD 5.9] years for the idiopathic SM group and 10.5 [SD 7.2] years for the NF2 group). Fourteen (9%) patients in the idiopathic SM group and 3 (20%) in the NF2 group had died at the last follow-up (p = 0.18). The 14 patients in the idiopathic SM group died at a mean time of 3.8 (SD 5.8) years after surgery compared with a mean time of 5.7 (SD 7.8) years after surgery in the NF2 group (p = 0.57). The overall mean time to death was 4.2 (SD 4.9) years (Table 2). OS curves between the idiopathic SM and NF2 groups are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1. Of the patients who experienced progression, the median PFS for those in the idiopathic SM group was 44.4 months (range: 8.2–152.1 months), whereas the median PFS for the NF2 group was 10.8 months (range 1.0–110.6 months) (p > 0.99) (Fig. 4A). In patients with WHO grade 1 tumors that progressed, the median PFS was 48.0 months (range 16.8–152.1 months) compared with 33.6 months (range 1.0–62.4 months) for those with WHO grade 2 tumors (p = 0.12) (Fig. 4B).

### Radiographic Analysis for All SM Patients

In our analysis assessing the relationship between various radiographic tumor characteristics and extent of resection, no statistically significant differences were found between tumors that were gross-totally and those that were subtotally resected. Of the 12 tumors that were subtotally resected, 4 (33%) were located ventrolaterally with respect to the spinal cord, 3 (25%) were lateral, 1 (8%) was dorsolateral, and 4 (33%) had unclear exact locations due to a lack of available preoperative imaging (Fig. 5A). The mean volume of tumors that were gross-totally resected was 3.4 (SD 4.9) cm3 compared with 5.8 (SD 4.9) cm3 for tumors that were subtotally resected (p = 0.2) (Fig. 5B). Fifty-two (34%) tumors that were gross-totally resected had an associated T2 cord signal compared with 5 (42%) that were subtotally resected (p = 0.75) (Fig. 5C). Thirty-eight (25%) tumors that were gross-totally resected had a positive dural tail sign, compared with 5 (42%) that were subtotally resected (p = 0.3) (Fig. 5D). Fifty-nine (38%) tumors that were gross-totally resected were calcified compared with 3 (25%) that were subtotally resected (p = 0.54) (Fig. 5E). Thirty-one (20%) of the tumors that were gross-totally resected were in a ventrolateral location compared with 4 (33%) that were subtotally resected (p = 0.74). There was a statistically significant difference in rates of radiographic progression between tumors that were gross-totally resected and those that were subtotally resected (p = 0.004) (Table 3, Fig. 5F). Finally, there were no significant differences in occurrence of T2 cord signal, dural tail sign, or calcification between patients who experienced tumor recurrence and those who did not. However, there was a statistically significant difference in tumor volume for patients who experienced tumor recurrence (mean 9.1 [SD 11.5] cm3) compared with those who did not (mean 3.25 [SD 4.6] 9.1 cm3) (p = 0.02).

### Cytogenetics Overview

Nineteen patients had cytology and genetics data available in their medical records, all of whom had surgery dates after 2015. Of these patients, 2 were in the NF2 group and 17 were in the idiopathic SM patient group, although 3 patients did have a separate intracranial tumor. The most common chromosomal abnormality across all 19 patients was monosomy 22 (n = 9). Of these 9 patients, 3 had copy number loss in the NF2 and SMARCB1 genes, while the remaining six had NF2 copy number loss only. The next most common chromosomal abnormality was chromosome 22 q-arm deletion (n = 3), all of which had copy number loss in the NF2 gene. The remaining chromosomal abnormalities were seen in only one patient each: chromosome 17 q-arm deletion with SMARCE1 copy number loss, single nucleotide variant in PIK3CA, single nucleotide variant in TSC2, polysomy 20, DMD exon deletion on the X-chromosome, and distal 6q deletion. An overview of the available genetic profiles is presented in Supplementary Table 1.

## Discussion

SMs are highly responsive to surgical treatment, with low rates of recurrence and a high likelihood of symptomatic improvement following resection. In the present study, patients with a concurrent NF2 diagnosis presented earlier, experienced progression earlier, and experienced progression more frequently, although there were no statistically significant differences in measured radiographic tumor characteristics compared with patients with idiopathic SM, and none of the measured radiographic characteristics were found to be significant predictors of maximal resection. While previous studies have focused on outcomes and ideal management of patients with SM, to our knowledge there has not been a dedicated analysis focused on these specific parameters and patient groups.2,4,7,8

It has been estimated that the median survival time for patients with NF2 is approximately 15 years following diagnosis, with 40% of patients estimated to die by the age of 50 years and virtually all by age 70 years.9,10 Furthermore, nearly 20% of patients who harbor an NF2 mutation will go on develop SMs, according to some studies.5,10 Based on our findings, it does not appear that SMs significantly impact the prognosis or disease progression of patients with NF2. While patients with NF2 can present with these tumors at an earlier age and experience higher rates of recurrence of these tumors specifically, it is likely that the intracranial disease burden and other systemic symptoms are more likely to directly cause morbidity and mortality in these patients compared with their SMs. Symptomatic burden is likely the most important factor to consider when deciding on management of these tumors. The rate of 5-year OS for idiopathic benign SMs is reportedly greater than 90%, suggesting that these tumors are associated with low mortality in otherwise healthy patients.11 Mortality in the present study was likely unrelated to a diagnosis of SM, as the average age at presentation of the 17 patients who died was 65.5 years.

Moreover, our findings with respect to progression following resection were consistent with the reported rates of recurrence for SMs, which range from 4% to 10% in the literature.7,12,13 It has been suggested that certain tumor characteristics, such as high Ki-67 and arachnoid invasion, are significant risk factors for recurrence of these tumors.14 Most patients who experienced progression in our cohort had either an initial STR or a diagnosis of NF2, which suggests that these two factors also predispose patients to experiencing recurrent disease. It is well established that SMs are highly accessible tumors with consistently favorable outcomes following initial surgery.2,8,13,15,16 Based on literature values and the 93% rate of GTR in the present study, resection should be considered front-line treatment if patients present with neurological decline and are reasonable surgical candidates.2,3 The majority of our patients experienced favorable functional and radiographic outcomes following initial resection without the need for follow-up interventions, all with low rates of surgical complications or associated deficits.

While factors like age, symptomatic burden at presentation, and systemic disease status are well documented influencers of surgical decision-making, literature regarding factors that may limit resection in this population is far less robust.3 Tumor characteristics including longitudinal and transverse extent, involvement of vascular and neural structures, and corresponding vertebral stability are critical to consider when establishing a surgical plan and approach for GTR of spinal cord tumors.17 To build on these fundamental concepts, we assessed the association between various radiographic characteristics with extent of resection and their prevalence in patients with NF2 versus idiopathic SMs. None of these factors were found to be statistically different between NF2 patients or idiopathic SM patients, nor were they found to influence the extent of resection. However, there was a statistically significant difference in rates of progression between patients with STR versus GTR, as expected. Studies with larger numbers of NF2-associated SMs may be warranted to further discern differences in radiographic tumor characteristics and their effects on extent of resection.

Multiple studies exist that have explored the role of chromosomal abnormalities in the development of SMs.18–22 In the present study, greater than 50% of idiopathic SMs that had available cytogenetics data were found to have NF2 deletions. The implications of leveraging chromosomal analyses like these in the management of CNS tumors are far reaching. In a recent study assessing the use of chromosomal copy number loss in time-to-recurrence predictions, Driver et al. demonstrated that the integrated grade for meningiomas, a tiered grading system based on mitotic count and various chromosomal losses, was able to more accurately identify meningioma patients at risk for recurrence compared with their WHO tumor grade.23 In a follow-up study of 94 SMs at our institution, 6 of 9 WHO grade 2 tumors were reclassified to low-risk integrated grade 1 following whole-genome copy number profiling assessment.24 These findings suggest that chromosomal analysis could provide a more nuanced biophysiological profile of these tumors, as the combination of copy number alterations and mitotic index has been shown to be a stronger predictor for tumor recurrence than WHO grade alone. Classifications and diagnostic schema based on precise molecular characteristics of tumors are therefore increasingly relevant in the treatment of CNS tumors, particularly SMs, in which a low WHO grade can still be assigned to tumors with borderline histopathology that may display aggressive molecular characteristics.

The present study has several limitations. Our paper was retrospective in design and was thus subject to biases in our patient selection and our ability to control for potential confounders in our analyses. While a relatively large number of SM patients were included in this study compared with similar case series, our NF2 patient group was comparatively small, which potentially limited our assessment of radiographic predictors in this population and the overall generalizability of our analysis. Furthermore, cytogenetics data was not available for the majority of the cohort, which limited our ability to incorporate molecular tumor characteristics into our analyses. These limitations should be considered when interpreting our results and in the planning of future studies aiming to assess outcomes and prognostic factors in SM patients.

## Conclusions

SMs are relatively common and benign tumors with a low rate of recurrence and favorable functional outcomes following surgery. Idiopathic SMs and NF2-associated SMs are radiographically similar and appear to be equally accessible for GTR. Patients who present with idiopathic SMs are less likely to present at a young age and experience disease recurrence than those with an NF2 diagnosis. Systemic disease including intracranial disease burden and cytogenetic profiles should be taken into consideration when developing individualized treatment plans for patients suffering from SMs.
